Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

hi everyone, i wanted to ask if we could look at a small change to how we handle the shared laundry room at the cooperative, especially on the busy days. i am not asking for a permanent rule right now, and i know some of you use the room at different hours because of work, school, or caring for family. it might be useful to try a clearer weekly plan for six weeks and then talk about whether it helped. if that feels like too much to take on, maybe we could start with just the weekend hours.

at the moment, the sign-up sheet is on the shelf beside the detergent cabinet, and people add their names in pencil. sometimes the writing is hard to read, and sometimes a time gets crossed out without a note, so another person cannot tell whether the machine is free or whether someone plans to come back. on Sunday, for example, there were three names beside the 10 a.m. slot and no note about which washers they meant. i do not know whether the sheet was confusing that day or whether people simply had a lot of laundry, but it seemed worth asking about a more consistent way to use it. could we put separate columns for washer one, washer two, and the large-capacity washer, and ask people to write a start time and an estimated finish time?

it may also help to have a simple way to mark a booking that is no longer needed. perhaps the person could draw one line through the name rather than erase it, so the next person can see the space is available and we can still tell what happened if there is a question. i would not want this to turn into a complicated reservation system. the main thing is that people can understand the sheet quickly, including anyone who is visiting the cooperative for the first time or does not know our usual habits. if someone has a better idea for keeping it clear, i would be glad to hear it.

there is a related question about the shared drying racks. we have six racks in the basement room, but two are close to the utility sink and can get splashed when the sink is being used. could we ask people to leave those two racks for items that can be moved easily, rather than for a full load that will need a long time to dry? i am not sure that this is a frequent problem, so perhaps we should first put a small note by the sink for a week and see whether people find it helpful. the note could say, “Please leave the two racks by the sink clear when you can; they may get splashed.” if that wording sounds too much like a rule, we could change it.

before deciding anything, could we also make a short list of the maintenance details that people should report? recently, i noticed that washer two sometimes takes a little longer to drain than the other machines. it did finish its cycle, and i do not know if there is an issue, but i would rather have people mention a change like that than assume everyone already knows. a report could include the machine number, the date, what the person noticed, and whether the cycle finished. that would give Marisol, who coordinates repairs, useful information without asking her to guess from a vague message such as “the washer is acting weird.” we should be clear that a report is not a diagnosis and that people should not open a machine or try to repair it themselves.

here is one possible outline for a trial plan, if people are comfortable considering it:
1. keep the existing sign-up sheet, but add a column for each washer and spaces for start and estimated finish times.
2. put a small, polite reminder beside the drying racks and the utility sink for one week, then ask whether it was useful or got in the way.
3. leave a maintenance notebook on the same shelf as the sign-up sheet, with a few blank lines for the machine number, date, observation, and cycle status.

we could ask two volunteers to check the sheet and notebook once a week, not to police anyone, but just to see whether the layout is understandable and whether supplies such as pencils are still there. if we do not have volunteers, or if that would add an unwanted task, we can skip that part and simply ask people for comments at the next meeting. i do not think anyone should be expected to monitor the room while doing their own laundry. the idea is to make shared use easier, not to create another job for members.

for the six-week trial, perhaps we could begin on the first Monday after our next monthly meeting, if the group agrees and someone has time to update the sheet. we could keep the existing laundry hours, the current machine-use limits, and the usual approach to detergent; this request is only about the sign-up sheet, rack reminder, and maintenance notes. if those dates do not work, or if the proposed plan needs to be shorter, i am open to another schedule. at the end, could we spend ten minutes at a meeting hearing what worked, what was confusing, and whether anything should be changed before continuing? i would appreciate your thoughts, especially from anyone who regularly uses the basement room in the evenings or on weekends.", "output": "Hi everyone, I wanted to ask whether we could consider a small change to how we manage the cooperative’s shared laundry room, especially on busy days. I’m not asking for a permanent rule right now, and I know some of you use the room at different times because of work, school, or caring for family. It might be useful to try a clearer weekly plan for six weeks and then discuss whether it helped. If that feels like too much to take on, perhaps we could start with just the weekend hours.

At the moment, the sign-up sheet is on the shelf beside the detergent cabinet, and people write their names in pencil. Sometimes the writing is hard to read, or a time is crossed out without a note, so others can’t tell whether the machine is free or someone plans to return. On Sunday, for example, there were three names beside the 10 a.m. slot, with no note about which washers they meant. I don’t know whether the sheet was confusing that day or people simply had a lot of laundry, but it seemed worth asking about a more consistent way to use it. Could we add separate columns for washer one, washer two, and the large-capacity washer, and ask people to write a start time and an estimated finish time?

It might also help to have a simple way to mark a booking that is no longer needed. Perhaps the person could draw a line through the name rather than erase it, so the next person can see that the space is available and we can still tell what happened if there’s a question. I wouldn’t want this to become a complicated reservation system. The main thing is for people to understand the sheet quickly, including anyone visiting the cooperative for the first time or unfamiliar with our usual habits. If someone has a better idea for keeping it clear, I’d be glad to hear it.

There’s a related question about the shared drying racks. We have six racks in the basement room, but two are close to the utility sink and can get splashed when it’s in use. Could we ask people to leave those two racks for items that can be moved easily, rather than using them for a full load that will take a long time to dry? I’m not sure this happens often, so perhaps we should first put a small note by the sink for a week and see whether people find it helpful. The note could say, “Please leave the two racks by the sink clear when you can; they may get splashed.” If that sounds too much like a rule, we could change the wording.

Before deciding anything, could we also make a short list of maintenance details people should report? Recently, I noticed that washer two sometimes takes a little longer to drain than the other machines. It did finish its cycle, and I don’t know whether there’s an issue, but I’d rather people mention a change like that than assume everyone already knows. A report could include the machine number, date, what the person noticed, and whether the cycle finished. That would give Marisol, who coordinates repairs, useful information without asking her to guess from a vague message such as “the washer is acting weird.” We should be clear that a report isn’t a diagnosis and that people shouldn’t open a machine or try to repair it themselves.

Here’s one possible outline for a trial plan, if people are comfortable considering it:
1. Keep the existing sign-up sheet, but add a column for each washer and spaces for start and estimated finish times.
2. Put a small, polite reminder beside the drying racks and utility sink for one week, then ask whether it was helpful or got in the way.
3. Leave a maintenance notebook on the same shelf as the sign-up sheet, with a few blank lines for the machine number, date, observation, and cycle status.

We could ask two volunteers to check the sheet and notebook once a week—not to police anyone, but simply to see whether the layout is understandable and whether supplies such as pencils are still there. If we don’t have volunteers, or if that would add an unwanted task, we can skip that part and simply ask people for comments at the next meeting. I don’t think anyone should be expected to monitor the room while doing their own laundry. The idea is to make shared use easier, not to create another job for members.

For the six-week trial, perhaps we could begin on the first Monday after our next monthly meeting, if the group agrees and someone has time to update the sheet. We could keep the existing laundry hours, current machine-use limits, and usual approach to detergent; this request is only about the sign-up sheet, rack reminder, and maintenance notes.
